a: The concept of zero evolved independently in several ancient civilizations. The earliest known use of zero as a placeholder was by the Babylonians around 300 BCE, who used a pair of angled wedges to indicate an empty position in their sexagesimal (base-60) number system. However, they did not treat zero as a number in its own right. The Mayans in Mesoamerica developed a shell-shaped symbol for zero around 4th century CE as part of their vigesimal (base-20) calendar system, using it both as a placeholder and as a number. The most significant development of zero as a full-fledged number came in ancient India around the 5th century CE. The Indian mathematician and astronomer Aryabhata (476-550 CE) used zero as a number in calculations, and Brahmagupta (598-668 CE) wrote the first formal rules for arithmetic operations involving zero, including addition, subtraction, and multiplication. The concept of zero spread from India to the Islamic world through trade and scholarship. The Persian mathematician Al-Khwarizmi (780-850 CE) introduced Indian numerals, including zero, to the Islamic world, and his work was later translated into Latin, bringing zero to medieval Europe. European mathematicians initially resisted the concept of zero, viewing it with suspicion as a foreign and potentially heretical idea. The word 'zero' derives from the Italian 'zero,' which came from the Arabic 'sifr,' meaning 'empty,' which in turn came from the Sanskrit 'shunya,' also meaning 'empty' or 'void.' The development of zero as both a placeholder and a number was a revolutionary mathematical achievement that enabled the development of algebra, calculus, and modern mathematics.
